17.stem: Stable angina is BEST distinguished from unstable angina by pain that:
choices: Occurs at rest and lasts hours without relief
Is predictable with exertion and eases with rest or nitroglycerin
Always means a completed myocardial infarction
Only occurs in patients under age 40
17.why: Stable angina is exertional and reproducible. Unstable angina is new, crescendo, or at rest — treat as ACS.

17.stem: Which presentation MOST suggests unstable angina?
choices: Chest pressure only after climbing two flights, relieved in two minutes by rest
New chest pressure at rest lasting 20 minutes with diaphoresis
Sharp chest wall pain reproduced by pressing on a rib
Brief palpitations after drinking coffee
17.why: Pain at rest, new onset, or worsening pattern = unstable. Transport and treat as ACS.

17.stem: Nitroglycerin is used with caution in suspected right-sided / inferior MI because these patients are often:
choices: Volume-overloaded and hypertensive
Preload-dependent, so vasodilation may cause severe hypotension
Immune to antiplatelet therapy
Unable to absorb sublingual medications
17.why: Right ventricular infarcts rely on preload. NTG drops venous return and BP can crash — check pressure and follow protocol.

17.stem: Which findings MOST suggest left-sided congestive heart failure?
choices: Dependent edema and JVD without dyspnea
Pulmonary crackles, orthopnea, and dyspnea
Isolated calf pain with a warm red leg
Wheezing after allergen exposure with hives
17.why: Left failure backs blood into the lungs — crackles, orthopnea, pink frothy sputum. Right failure shows systemic congestion.

17.stem: Peripheral edema, ascites, and jugular venous distention without prominent pulmonary crackles MOST suggest:
choices: Left-sided heart failure primarily
Right-sided heart failure or elevated venous pressure
Simple dehydration
An isolated asthma attack
17.why: Right heart / venous backup shows as JVD, edema, and hepatic congestion. Many patients have both sides failing.

17.stem: Hypertensive emergency differs from hypertensive urgency mainly because emergency includes:
choices: Any reading over 140/90 on a single check
End-organ damage signs such as stroke, ACS, or acute pulmonary edema
Only anxiety without neurologic change
A normal neurologic exam and no symptoms
17.why: Urgency = very high BP without acute organ injury. Emergency = high BP plus damage (neuro, cardiac, renal).

17.stem: For a very high blood pressure reading without acute end-organ findings, the EMT should:
choices: Rapidly lower BP with multiple nitroglycerin doses
Keep the patient calm, monitor, and transport for evaluation
Have the patient take an extra home antihypertensive immediately
Apply an AED prophylactically
17.why: EMTs do not aggressively chase BP numbers. Minimize stimulation, reassess, and let the hospital control titrated drops.

17.stem: An AED is indicated when the patient is:
choices: Alert with chest pain and a strong radial pulse
Unresponsive, pulseless, and not breathing normally
Awake with a pulse of 40 and dizziness
Conscious with atrial fibrillation history
17.why: AEDs treat sudden cardiac arrest. A pulse means ACS/bradycardia care — not defibrillation.

17.stem: When applying AED pads to an adult, you should:
choices: Place both pads stacked directly over the sternum
Use manufacturer pad placement (typically anterolateral or anterior-posterior) on dry bare skin
Apply pads over a wet shirt to save time
Place pads only on the back so bystanders cannot see them
17.why: Bare, dry skin; follow pad diagrams. Moisture and clothing reduce energy delivery and risk arcing.

17.stem: While the AED is analyzing the rhythm, rescuers should:
choices: Continue chest compressions at full rate
Ensure no one is touching the patient
Shake the patient to confirm unresponsiveness again
Give two rescue breaths during analysis
17.why: Movement ruins analysis and risks shocking a rescuer. Clear the patient; resume CPR immediately after.

17.stem: After ROSC (return of spontaneous circulation), the MOST appropriate EMT priority is:
choices: Stop all monitoring because the emergency is over
Support airway/breathing, reassess vitals frequently, and transport while watching for re-arrest
Sit the patient upright and have them walk to the stretcher
Remove the AED pads immediately in all cases
17.why: ROSC patients are fragile. Optimize oxygenation/ventilation, keep pads ready, and treat post-arrest shock.

17.stem: The usual adult aspirin dose for suspected ACS that EMTs assist with is:
choices: 81 mg swallowed enteric-coated with water
324 mg (commonly four 81 mg) chewed
650 mg of acetaminophen chewed
One baby aspirin placed under the tongue
17.why: Chewed non–enteric-coated aspirin (160–325 mg; often 324 mg) gets antiplatelet effect faster.

17.stem: In OPQRST for chest pain, asking whether anything makes the pain better or worse assesses:
choices: Onset
Provocation / palliation
Quality
Time only
17.why: P = what provokes or palliates. O is onset; Q is quality; R is region/radiation; S severity; T timing.

17.stem: Asking a chest-pain patient to describe the pain as crushing, sharp, or burning is assessing:
choices: Severity on a 0–10 scale
Quality of the pain
Radiation only
Past medical history
17.why: Quality is the character of the pain. Severity is the number; radiation is where it travels.

17.stem: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and hypoxia after prolonged immobility can mimic ACS and MOST suggests:
choices: Pulmonary embolism
Stable angina relieved only by rest
Simple costochondritis
Gastroesophageal reflux alone
17.why: PE is a classic ACS mimic — sudden SOB ± chest pain, risk factors like travel or DVT. Support ABCs and go.

17.stem: Sudden tearing chest or back pain with unequal pulses or BP between arms MOST suggests:
choices: Esophageal spasm
Aortic dissection
Stable angina only
Musculoskeletal strain
17.why: Dissection = abrupt tearing pain, often radiating to the back, with pulse/BP asymmetry. Gentle handling, rapid transport.

17.stem: For suspected aortic dissection, which action is MOST appropriate for the EMT?
choices: Give aspirin and nitroglycerin as for typical ACS
Keep the patient calm, support ABCs, avoid unnecessary jolting, and rapid transport
Deeply palpate the abdomen to confirm a pulsatile mass
Have the patient ambulate to see if pain eases
17.why: Nitro/ASA can worsen hypotension/bleeding risk. Minimize stimulation and get them to definitive care.

17.stem: An implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is designed to:
choices: Prevent all forms of chest pain
Detect and shock certain lethal ventricular arrhythmias from inside the body
Replace the need for CPR if the patient collapses
Always keep heart rate above 100
17.why: ICDs treat VT/VF internally. If the patient is pulseless, still do CPR and use an AED — pad away from the device.

17.stem: When defibrillating a patient with an ICD or pacemaker bulge, pad placement should:
choices: Be placed directly over the generator for best conduction
Be kept at least about an inch away from the implanted device
Be withheld entirely to protect the device
Use pediatric pads on all adults with devices
17.why: Offset pads from the generator and treat the arrest normally. Do not withhold life-saving shocks.

17.stem: Compared with typical angina, myocardial infarction pain is MORE likely to:
choices: Resolve after two minutes of rest every time
Persist longer and not fully relieve with rest or a single nitro dose
Be reproduced only by pressing on the chest wall
Occur exclusively in teenagers
17.why: MI ischemia lasts; tissue is dying. Unrelieved or prolonged pain needs ACS care and transport.

17.stem: Oxygen for a chest-pain patient with SpO2 98% on room air who is comfortable should generally be:
choices: Withheld or titrated — routine high-flow O2 is not required if not hypoxic
Delivered by nonrebreather at 15 L/min for every ACS patient
Given only by bag-mask ventilation
Replaced by having them breathe into a paper bag
17.why: Give O2 for hypoxia, distress, or shock. Hyperoxia is not a default ACS treatment for normoxic patients.

17.stem: In the adult Chain of Survival, after recognizing arrest and activating EMS, the NEXT critical link is:
choices: Immediate high-quality CPR
Drawing blood for labs
Obtaining a full SAMPLE history before compressions
Waiting for ALS medications
17.why: Recognition → activation → CPR → defibrillation → ALS → post-arrest care. Compressions start now.

17.stem: High-quality adult CPR includes all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Compressions about 2 inches deep at 100–120/min
Full chest recoil between compressions
Minimal interruptions
Frequent pulse checks every 5–10 seconds throughout
17.why: Constant pulse hunting kills perfusion. Check briefly at appropriate intervals; keep the ratio and depth right.

17.stem: A conscious patient with severe pulmonary edema from CHF is BEST positioned:
choices: Fully supine with legs elevated
Upright / sitting, legs dangling if tolerated
Prone to improve oxygenation
Trendelenburg to raise blood pressure
17.why: Sitting reduces venous return and eases work of breathing. Flat positions worsen orthopnea.

17.stem: Before assisting with prescribed nitroglycerin for chest pain, the EMT must confirm all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: The medication is prescribed for this patient
Systolic BP meets protocol minimum (often ≥100)
No recent PDE-5 inhibitor use
A confirmed STEMI on a 12-lead the EMT interpreted alone
17.why: EMTs assist based on protocol/medical direction — not on independently diagnosing STEMI. Check Rx, BP, and PDE-5.

17.stem: Aspirin for suspected ACS should be withheld when the patient has:
choices: A known aspirin allergy or active significant bleeding
Taken acetaminophen earlier today
A history of hypertension that is controlled
Eaten breakfast within the last hour
17.why: Allergy and active bleeding (or other protocol exclusions) block ASA. Food and HTN are not automatic stops.

17.stem: Cardiac ischemic pain commonly radiates to all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Left arm or both arms
Jaw or neck
Epigastrium / upper abdomen
The distal toes exclusively
17.why: Classic radiation is arm, jaw, neck, back, or epigastrium — not isolated toe pain.

17.stem: Beck’s triad (hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds) after chest trauma suggests:
choices: Cardiac tamponade
Simple bronchitis
Stable angina
Hyperventilation syndrome
17.why: Fluid around the heart impairs filling. Rapid transport — this is obstructive shock physiology.

17.stem: Which clue leans MORE toward abdominal aortic aneurysm / dissection than typical ACS?
choices: Crushing substernal pressure relieved by one nitro
Sudden tearing abdominal or back pain with unequal femoral pulses
Reproducible chest wall tenderness after coughing
Burning epigastric pain after spicy food that eases with antacids
17.why: Tearing back/abdomen pain + pulse deficit screams vascular catastrophe, not classic coronary ischemia.

17.stem: For a witnessed adult collapse that is pulseless, the AED advises a shock. Your NEXT action is:
choices: Clear the patient and deliver the shock, then immediately resume CPR
Check a carotid pulse for a full minute before shocking
Give two minutes of rescue breathing only
Wait for ALS to confirm the rhythm on a monitor
17.why: Shock promptly, then CPR. Do not delay defibrillation for prolonged pulse checks.

17.stem: If the AED advises “no shock,” the EMT should:
choices: Assume the patient has a pulse and stop CPR
Resume high-quality CPR immediately and reassess per protocol
Deliver three stacked shocks anyway
Turn the AED off permanently
17.why: No-shock rhythms (asystole/PEA) still need CPR. Keep the AED on for the next analysis cycle.

17.stem: A patient with suspected ACS who remains symptomatic should be:
choices: Encouraged to walk to reduce anxiety
Moved with minimal exertion and transported promptly, preferably to cardiac-capable care per protocol
Left sitting at home if one nitro helped slightly
Required to sign a refusal after any aspirin dose
17.why: Reduce myocardial demand: carry them, keep calm, early notification, right destination when available.

17.stem: Cool, pale, diaphoretic skin in a patient with crushing chest pressure MOST suggests:
choices: Sympathetic stress from significant cardiac ischemia or evolving shock
A normal finding in all healthy adults
Heat exhaustion only
That the pain is definitely musculoskeletal
17.why: Diaphoresis with ACS symptoms is a sick finding — think ischemia and possible pump failure.

17.stem: After assisting with the maximum protocol doses of nitroglycerin without relief, the EMT should:
choices: Continue stacking extra tablets every 30 seconds
Reassess vitals, continue supportive ACS care, and transport
Switch to ibuprofen for pain control
Have the patient stand to redistribute blood flow
17.why: Respect dose limits and hypotension risk. Support ABCs, ASA if indicated, and go.

17.stem: When protocol allows CPAP for CHF/pulmonary edema, the main benefit for the EMT-level provider is:
choices: Forcing fluid out of the alveoli by positive airway pressure and reducing work of breathing
Replacing the need for oxygen entirely
Defibrillating lethal arrhythmias
Diagnosing STEMI without a 12-lead
17.why: CPAP stents airways and decreases preload/afterload burden. Watch BP and mental status; it’s not for every patient.

17.stem: An elderly patient with near-syncope, a slow pulse, and chest discomfort should make you MOST concerned for:
choices: A primary psychiatric panic attack only
A cardiac conduction or ischemic problem needing rapid evaluation
A simple ear infection
Benign dehydration that never warrants transport
17.why: Brady + near-faint + ischemic symptoms = time-sensitive cardiac. Support ABCs and transport.

17.stem: All of the following are reasonable ACS treatment priorities for the EMT, EXCEPT:
choices: Aspirin when indicated by protocol
Position of comfort and limited exertion
Assisting prescribed nitro when criteria are met
Administering a fibrinolytic drug in the field without medical direction
17.why: Fibrinolysis is hospital/ALS-system dependent. EMTs focus on ASA, NTG assist, O2 as needed, and rapid transport.

17.stem: Bilateral pitting ankle edema that develops gradually in a cardiac patient MOST often reflects:
choices: Chronic venous congestion from heart failure
An acute isolated asthma attack
A fresh arterial embolism to both feet
Normal findings after one night of rest
17.why: Dependent edema is a right-sided/chronic CHF clue. Correlate with dyspnea, weight gain, and meds.

17.stem: After ROSC, if the patient remains unresponsive with inadequate breathing, you should:
choices: Provide assisted ventilations with oxygen and reassess frequently
Assume breathing will normalize without support
Place them prone without an airway plan
Give oral fluids to raise blood pressure
17.why: Post-arrest brains and hearts need oxygen. Support ventilation; avoid both hypoxia and excessive hyperventilation.

17.stem: For a chest-pain patient, asking about prior heart attacks, stents, or heart failure mainly gathers the “P” in SAMPLE — which is:
choices: Pulse oximetry reading
Past medical history / pertinent history
Provocation of pain
Primary survey findings only
17.why: SAMPLE’s P is past/pertinent medical history. OPQRST’s P is provocation — different mnemonics.

18.stem: Most strokes are ischemic, meaning they are caused by:
choices: Bleeding into brain tissue or subarachnoid space
Blockage of a cerebral artery by clot or embolus
A brief absence seizure
Middle-ear infection alone
18.why: Ischemic = vessel occlusion. Hemorrhagic = bleeding. Both need rapid transport; do not give ASA in the field for stroke.

18.stem: Which presentation MORE strongly suggests hemorrhagic rather than typical ischemic stroke?
choices: Gradual mild arm weakness over days without headache
Sudden severe “worst headache,” vomiting, and rapid decline in LOC
Transient blurry vision that resolved yesterday
Isolated tinnitus after a loud concert
18.why: Thunderclap headache, vomiting, and sudden coma raise hemorrhage concern. Still use stroke screens and go fast.

18.stem: Compared with FAST, BE-FAST adds assessment of:
choices: Blood glucose and fever only
Balance and Eyes (vision) changes
Breath sounds and edema
Blood pressure and ECG
18.why: B = balance problems; E = eye/vision changes. Still Face, Arm, Speech, Time.

18.stem: The Cincinnati Prehospital Stroke Scale assesses which three findings?
choices: Facial droop, arm drift, and abnormal speech
Pupil size, grip strength, and gait only
Blood pressure, pulse, and SpO2 only
Memory, orientation, and cranial nerve XII only
18.why: One abnormal finding is a positive screen. Pair it with last known well and glucose.

18.stem: A positive arm-drift finding on stroke screening means:
choices: Both arms stay up equally for the full test
One arm drifts down or cannot be raised compared with the other
The patient refuses to cooperate for any reason
Grip strength is equal bilaterally
18.why: Pronator drift or inability to hold one arm up = abnormal. Document which side.

18.stem: Absence seizures are BEST described as:
choices: Brief staring spells with little or no convulsive movement, often in children
Prolonged full-body tonic-clonic activity lasting over 5 minutes
Only nocturnal sleepwalking
Stroke that always leaves permanent paralysis
18.why: Absence = short “blank out.” Tonic-clonic has stiffening then jerking of the whole body.

18.stem: A generalized tonic-clonic seizure typically includes:
choices: Only a brief stare lasting 2–3 seconds
Loss of consciousness with tonic stiffening followed by clonic jerking
Preserved conversation throughout the event
Voluntary purposeful fighting movements only
18.why: Tonic = rigid; clonic = rhythmic jerks. Protect the airway/environment and time it.

18.stem: An aura before a seizure is:
choices: A sensory warning (smell, taste, vision, feeling) that a seizure may begin
The postictal recovery period
Proof the event cannot be epileptic
Always a hemorrhagic stroke
18.why: Auras are simple partial / warning symptoms. Ask witnesses what happened just before the event.

18.stem: For a child with a simple febrile seizure that has stopped, EMT care focuses on:
choices: Packing the child in ice until shivering starts
Supporting ABCs, gentle cooling if hot, checking glucose per protocol, and transport/evaluation
Forcing oral antipyretics into an unresponsive child
Restraining them prone until fever resolves
18.why: Most febrile seizures are brief. Airway, temperature control without overcooling, and rule out worse causes.

18.stem: A severe migraine can mimic stroke. The safest prehospital approach is to:
choices: Assume migraine and leave the patient home if they have a headache history
Treat new focal deficits as possible stroke until proven otherwise and transport
Give aspirin for every headache to prevent stroke
Hyperventilate the patient to reduce intracranial pressure
18.why: History of migraine does not cancel a new facial droop or arm weakness. Err toward stroke pathway.

18.stem: AEIOU-TIPS is a mnemonic used to remember causes of:
choices: Chest pain only
Altered mental status
Isolated ankle sprain
Normal pediatric growth
18.why: Alcohol/acidosis, Epilepsy, Insulin, Overdose, Uremia, Trauma/temp, Infection, Psych, Stroke/shock — AMS map.

18.stem: In AEIOU-TIPS, the “I” MOST commonly reminds EMTs to consider:
choices: Immobilization of every joint
Insulin-related problems (hypoglycemia / hyperglycemia)
Insect bites only
Iron deficiency as the sole AMS cause
18.why: Check blood glucose early. Hypoglycemia is reversible and mimics stroke, seizure, and intoxication.

18.stem: On the Glasgow Coma Scale, spontaneous eye opening scores:
18.why: Eyes: 4 spontaneous, 3 to voice, 2 to pain, 1 none. Know the ranges for reporting trend.

18.stem: The highest possible Glasgow Coma Scale total is:
18.why: E4 + V5 + M6 = 15. Three is the minimum (no response in any category).

18.stem: All of the following are GCS components, EXCEPT:
choices: Eye opening
Verbal response
Motor response
Blood pressure category
18.why: GCS is neurologic responsiveness only — not vital signs. Still report BP separately.

18.stem: Fever, headache, altered mental status, and neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity) MOST suggest:
choices: Meningitis or CNS infection until proven otherwise
A simple tension headache
Uncomplicated seasonal allergies
Stable angina
18.why: Protect yourself (BSI), support ABCs, minimize stimulation, and transport — bacterial meningitis is time-critical.

18.stem: A conscious suspected stroke patient who is not in shock is usually transported:
choices: With the head elevated slightly (about 30°) if protocol allows and airway is protected
In Trendelenburg with legs high
Prone to protect the airway
Standing to test balance repeatedly
18.why: Slight head elevation may help ICP/airway comfort. Protect vomit risk; do not fatigue them with walking tests.

18.stem: Why do EMTs generally NOT give aspirin for suspected stroke in the field?
choices: Aspirin has no effect on platelets
Hemorrhagic stroke cannot be ruled out without imaging, and ASA could worsen bleeding
Aspirin is only for children
Stroke patients never have ischemic disease
18.why: Hospital CT distinguishes bleed vs clot. Field ASA is for ACS pathways, not undifferentiated stroke.

18.stem: Sudden unilateral facial droop and one-sided arm weakness is BEST described as a:
choices: Focal neurologic deficit
Global metabolic finding only
Normal aging change
Psychiatric conversion that never needs transport
18.why: Focal findings point to stroke/TIA territory. Still check glucose — metabolic problems can mimic.

18.stem: Which history MOST favors seizure over primary stroke as the cause of a transient deficit?
choices: Witnessed convulsions followed by gradual awakening with tongue bite
Sudden aphasia and hemiparesis without any convulsive activity
Thunderclap headache with neck stiffness only
Progressive dementia over years
18.why: Convulsions + postictal course suggest seizure. Still assess for stroke if deficits persist or onset is unclear.

18.stem: A simple partial (focal aware) seizure may present as:
choices: Localized twitching or sensory symptoms with preserved awareness
Always full loss of consciousness and incontinence
Only cardiac arrest
A normal EEG by definition without symptoms
18.why: Focal seizures can stay in one body part. Protect the patient; they may progress to generalized activity.

18.stem: The FIRST priorities for any markedly altered patient are:
choices: Airway, breathing, circulation, and rapid identification of reversible causes
A complete 12-lead before opening the airway
Detailed family counseling before vital signs
Having them stand to assess orthostatics immediately
18.why: ABCs first, then glucose/oxygen/naloxone per protocol. History follows once life threats are handled.

18.stem: Cushing’s triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular respirations) suggests:
choices: Rising intracranial pressure
Simple dehydration
Anaphylaxis
Hyperglycemia only
18.why: Late ICP sign. Support airway, avoid hypotonic fluids/overventilation extremes, rapid transport.

18.stem: When local protocol designates stroke centers, a patient with a positive stroke screen and known last known well should be:
choices: Taken to the closest facility capable of rapid stroke evaluation per protocol, with early notification
Taken home if deficits improve in the ambulance
Held on scene until deficits fully resolve
Routed only after a two-hour on-scene neuro consult
18.why: Time is brain. Notify early, minimize scene time, and follow destination policies.

18.stem: A patient who opens eyes to pain, groans incomprehensibly, and withdraws from pain has a GCS closest to:
18.why: E2 + V2 + M4 = 8. Know how to add the three scores for clear handoff reports.

18.stem: During or immediately after a generalized seizure, oxygen is indicated when:
choices: The patient is cyanotic, hypoxic, or has inadequate breathing
Every seizing patient must get a nonrebreather even with SpO2 99% and good color
Only if the family requests it
Never, because oxygen causes seizures
18.why: Support oxygenation for hypoxia/poor ventilation. Do not force a mask that obstructs during thrashing.

18.stem: A patient who ignores the left side of space and collides into objects on that side may have:
choices: Unilateral neglect, often from right-hemisphere stroke
Normal vision in all cases
Only an orthopedic problem
Proof of malingering
18.why: Neglect is a neuro deficit. Protect them from injury and include it in your stroke report.

18.stem: Classic meningitis findings include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Fever
Neck stiffness
Photophobia / headache
Painless isolated ankle swelling as the primary sign
18.why: Think fever + headache + stiff neck ± rash/AMS. Isolated ankle edema is not a meningitis hallmark.

18.stem: In AEIOU-TIPS, trauma and temperature problems are grouped under which letter?
choices: A
E
T
S
18.why: T = trauma / temperature (and sometimes tumor). Always consider head injury and hypo/hyperthermia.

18.stem: For most prehospital stroke patients, EMTs should:
choices: Aggressively lower very high BP with multiple nitroglycerin doses
Monitor BP, avoid unnecessary BP-lowering meds, and transport
Ignore BP entirely because it never matters in stroke
Require the patient to take extra home antihypertensives before transport
18.why: Permissive hypertension is often intentional until imaging. Do not crash the pressure in the field.

18.stem: Febrile seizures are MOST associated with:
choices: Young children during a rapid rise in body temperature from illness
Only adults over 65 with hypertension
Always structural brain tumors
Cardiac arrest rhythms exclusively
18.why: Typically 6 months–5 years with fever. Still evaluate — first seizures need medical workup.

18.stem: Slurred speech from weak articulating muscles (often with facial droop) is called:
choices: Dysarthria
Anosmia
Tinnitus
Vertigo only
18.why: Dysarthria is motor speech impairment; aphasia is language. Both can appear on stroke screens as “abnormal speech.”

18.stem: Sudden inability to walk straight or sit upright without falling, with new dizziness, should prompt:
choices: BE-FAST / posterior stroke consideration and rapid transport
Reassurance that balance problems are never neurologic
A field diagnosis of inner-ear infection only, with refusal encouraged
Immediate aspirin for presumed migraine
18.why: Balance/eye findings catch posterior circulation strokes FAST can miss. Treat as stroke until proven otherwise.

18.stem: Serial GCS assessments are valuable mainly because they:
choices: Replace the need for vital signs
Show improvement or deterioration over time for handoff and decisions
Diagnose the exact brain lesion without imaging
Are only used in psychiatric facilities
18.why: A falling GCS means the patient is getting worse — recheck ABCs and speed transport.

18.stem: After a convulsive seizure, if the patient is breathing adequately but remains unresponsive, a good position is:
choices: Lateral recovery position to protect the airway from secretions
Sitting bolt upright forced against their will
Prone with the face buried in a pillow
Standing with assistance immediately
18.why: Recovery position drains vomit/saliva. Keep suction ready and watch for another seizure.

18.stem: Common risk factors for ischemic stroke include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Atrial fibrillation
Hypertension and atherosclerosis
Prior TIA
Being a healthy toddler with no medical history
18.why: AF emboli, HTN, and prior TIA drive adult ischemic stroke risk. Toddlers are not the typical demographic.

18.stem: Pinpoint pupils, slow respirations, and unresponsiveness in AEIOU-TIPS thinking MOST suggest:
choices: Opioid overdose (the “O”)
Isolated hyperglycemia without respiratory depression
A migraine aura only
Hyperthermia from heat stroke exclusively
18.why: Support ventilation and give naloxone per protocol. Do not skip the airway for a drug history debate.

18.stem: On a clear stroke alert call, scene time should generally be:
choices: Minimized after ABCs, glucose, stroke scale, and last known well are obtained
Extended for a complete head-to-toe physical lasting 30 minutes
Spent waiting to see if symptoms resolve completely
Used mainly to obtain a signed DNR before any assessment
18.why: Load-and-go mentality after critical data. Hospitals need clock time and a focused neuro report.

18.stem: “Petit mal” is an older term that usually refers to:
choices: Absence seizures
Status epilepticus only
Hemorrhagic stroke
Syncope from dehydration
18.why: Petit mal ≈ absence. Grand mal ≈ tonic-clonic. Use modern terms on reports when you can.

18.stem: Appropriate EMT actions for suspected stroke include all of the following, EXCEPT:
choices: Checking blood glucose
Performing a Cincinnati or BE-FAST screen
Documenting last known well
Giving oral glucose to every stroke patient regardless of glucose reading
18.why: Treat documented hypoglycemia — do not sugar-load a normoglycemic or hyperglycemic stroke patient.
